verdict.rationale: Two unranked patterns spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) govern this proposition. Pattern one ties the saving outcome to a named, heard, and confessed object. Romans 10:14-17 builds a four-link chain (calling presupposes believing, believing presupposes hearing, hearing presupposes a preacher, summed up as 'faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ' (hē pistis ex akoēs, hē de akoē dia rhēmatos Christou)). John 3:18 grounds standing condemnation on not having believed 'in the name of the only-begotten Son' (eis to onoma tou monogenous huiou), where 'only-begotten' (monogenes) means 'one-of-a-kind'. Acts 4:12 excludes any other name. Pattern two states that in every nation the God-fearer who works righteousness is 'acceptable' (dektos) to God (Acts 10:35), that Gentiles without the law do by nature 'the things of the law' (ta tou nomou) with conscience excusing at the judgment (Romans 2:14-16), and that faith justified Abraham apart from gospel content (Romans 4:3-5) while Hebrews 11:6 demands only faith that God is and rewards seekers. The vocabulary does not rank these patterns or settle the cases of those never evangelized and those who lived before the incarnation, so the proposition's exclusive scope is underdetermined at the level of words.

scripture.reasoning: An 'if-then' (conditional) construction with 'if' (ean) governs two parallel subjunctive verbs, 'you confess' (homologēsēs) with the mouth and 'you believe' (pisteusēs) in the heart, both leading to the future passive 'you will be saved' (sōthēsē). The object of confession is 'the Lord Jesus' (kyrion Iēsoun), the named historical referent. The verbal pair binds outward profession and inward trust to the saving outcome.

Four 'how?' (pōs) questions build a causal chain in reverse: 'calling upon' (epikaleō) presupposes believing, believing presupposes hearing, hearing presupposes a preacher. The clause 'how will they believe in him whom they have not heard?' (pōs de pisteusōsin hou ouk ēkousan) makes prior hearing a stated prerequisite of the saving response, and the rhetorical questions assume each prior link is required.

Summary clause, 'so then, faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ' (ara hē pistis ex akoēs, hē de akoē dia rhēmatos Christou). 'Faith' (pistis) is sourced 'from' (ex) 'hearing' (akoē), and 'hearing' (akoē) comes 'through' (dia) the spoken 'word' (rhēma) of Christ. The chain anchors saving faith to an externally proclaimed content.

Contrastive present participles: 'the one believing' (ho pisteuōn) is not judged, but 'the one not believing' (ho mē pisteuōn) is judged already ('has already been judged' (ēdē kekritai), a perfect passive (a completed action whose result still stands) marking a standing verdict). The causal 'because' (hoti) clause names the content, 'in the name of the only-begotten Son of God' (eis to onoma tou monogenous huiou tou theou), where 'only-begotten' (monogenes) means 'one-of-a-kind'. Failure to believe in this specific name is the stated ground of condemnation.

Antithetic pair: 'the one believing in the Son' (ho pisteuōn eis ton huion) has eternal life, 'the one disobeying the Son' (ho apeithōn tō huiō) will not see life ('shall not see life' (ouk opsetai zōēn)). The opposite of believing here is 'to refuse to be persuaded or to disobey' (apeitheō), which presents the negative case as active rejection of a presented Son rather than mere non-exposure.

Double exclusion: 'there is no salvation in anyone else' (ouk estin en allō oudeni hē sōtēria) negates salvation in any other, and 'neither is there any other name under heaven given among men' (oude onoma estin heteron hypo ton ouranon to dedomenon en anthrōpois) excludes any other name given among humans. The clause forecloses an alternate name but speaks of the means of salvation, not explicitly of every person's required knowing access to that name.

Predicate nominative (a noun completing a 'X is Y' statement) self-identification, 'I am the way' (egō eimi hē hodos), followed by 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (oudeis erchetai pros ton patera ei mē di' emou). The exclusive 'through me' (di' emou) marks Christ as the sole channel to the Father. The clause fixes the means as Christ but the words do not specify whether access to that means requires explicit knowledge of him.

Balanced conditional ('if-then' clause), 'the one having the Son has the life, the one not having the Son of God does not have the life' (ho echōn ton huion echei tēn zōēn, ho mē echōn ton huion tou theou tēn zōēn ouk echei). Possessing life is co-extensive with possessing the Son. The verb 'to have' (echō) frames the link as having or not having the Son, leaving open how having is mediated.

'In every nation the one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him' (en panti ethnei ho phoboumenos auton kai ergazomenos dikaiosynēn dektos autō estin). The universal scope ('in every nation' (panti ethnei)) plus the participial subject (the one fearing God and working righteousness) is predicated 'acceptable' (dektos), welcome to him. 'Acceptable' (dektos) occurs only five times in the canon (Philippians 4:18, 2 Corinthians 6:2, Luke 4:19, Luke 4:24, here), where it means welcome or acceptable rather than saved, so its force here is not pinned at the lexical level to final salvation.

Same narrative, 'everyone believing in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name' (panta ton pisteuonta eis auton aphesin hamartiōn labein dia tou onomatos autou). 'Forgiveness' (aphesis) is received 'through the name' (dia tou onomatos) through believing in him. Verses 35 and 43 sit in one episode: one calls the God-fearer 'acceptable' (dektos) before proclamation, the other ties forgiveness to believing the name, and the text does not rank at the lexical level 'acceptable' (dektos) against the subsequent 'believe' (pisteuō) requirement.

'Gentiles not having the law by nature do the things of the law' (ethnē ta mē nomon echonta physei ta tou nomou poiōsin). Gentiles lacking the written law do 'by nature' (physei, dative of manner (a noun in the 'in-the-manner-of' grammatical form)) the things of the law and are a law to themselves. The clause grants a category of law-keeping apart from special revelation but does not state that this confers saving access.

'Their conscience also bearing witness, and between themselves their thoughts accusing or even defending them' (symmartyrousēs autōn tēs syneidēseōs kai metaxy allēlōn tōn logismōn katēgorountōn ē kai apologoumenōn). 'Conscience' (syneidēsis) co-witnesses and thoughts 'accuse' (katēgoreō) or even 'defend' (apologeomai). The disjunction 'or' (ē) leaves both outcomes open at the judgment, so the verse describes a real defending verdict for some but does not specify its saving weight.

'But to the one not working, but believing on the one who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness' (tō de mē ergazomenō, pisteuonti de epi ton dikaiounta ton asebē, logizetai hē pistis autou eis dikaiosynēn). Abraham (Romans 4:3) is justified by 'believing' (pisteuō) whose stated object is the God who justifies the ungodly, not the historical content of the incarnation. The words fix faith as the instrument but its explicit object here predates gospel proclamation.

'For the one approaching God must believe that he is and is a rewarder of those who seek him out' (pisteusai gar dei ton proserchomenon tō theō hoti estin kai tois ekzētousin auton misthapodotēs ginetai). Faith is required ('it is necessary' (dei)), but the stated propositional object is that God is and rewards those who seek him out. 'Rewarder' (misthapodotēs) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, only here), so the precise content demanded cannot be triangulated, and the named object is God-who-rewards rather than the historical Jesus.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'Acceptable' (dektos, G1184) in Acts 10:35 predicates the God-fearer of every nation as acceptable to God, but the word occurs only five times in the canon and elsewhere means welcome or acceptable (an offering, a favorable season), not saved. Within the same episode Acts 10:43 ties forgiveness to believing in the name, and the Spirit falls only after Peter's proclamation (Acts 10:44). The vocabulary therefore presents two statements in one narrative, acceptable-before-hearing and forgiveness-through-believing-the-name, and does not rank them at the lexical level, which is precisely why the case of the never-evangelized stays open.

'By nature' (physei, G5449) governs Gentiles without the law doing the things of the law, and 'conscience' (syneidēsis, G4893) 'accuses' (katēgoreō) or 'defends' (apologeomai) at the judgment. The disjunction 'or' (ē) keeps a defending verdict genuinely possible for some, but the passage never attaches the word 'save' (sōzō) or 'life' (zōē) to that defending verdict, so the words establish a non-revelatory law-awareness without stating that it grants saving access. The text leaves the saving weight of conscience underdetermined.

'Believe' (pisteuō) justifies Abraham with 'it is reckoned as righteousness' (logizetai eis dikaiosynēn), but the explicit object of his faith is the promise and the God who justifies the ungodly, content available before the incarnation. The words fix faith as the saving instrument yet show a saving faith whose explicit propositional object was not the historical Jesus, which the proposition's wording (faith in the historical Jesus) does not accommodate without supplement.

'It is necessary' (dei) plus 'to believe' (pisteusai) makes faith mandatory for the one approaching God, but the stated object is that God is and is a rewarder of seekers. 'Rewarder' (misthapodotēs, G3406) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), so its content cannot be triangulated, and the verse defines required faith by God-who-rewards rather than by explicit Christ-knowledge, leaving the object of faith for the pre-incarnation case and for the never-evangelized case open at the level of words.

variants.note: No variant units were flagged in the supplied bundle for Romans 10:9-17, John 3:18, John 3:36, or Acts 4:12, and these passages fall outside the ingested ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window (3 John). The minor apparatus sigla visible on the surface forms ('your' (sou), 'they hear' (akousōsin), 'they believe' (pisteusōsin), 'they call upon' (epikalesōntai), 'just as' (kathōs), 'preaching good news' (euangelizomenōn), 'they preach' (kēryxōsin), 'the' (ta), 'of Christ' (Christou), 'by' (hypo), 'nor' (oude), 'and' (de)) touch word order and auxiliary phrasing but not the load-bearing words 'believe' (pisteuō), 'confess' (homologeō), 'call upon' (epikaleō), 'name' (onoma), 'salvation' (sōtēria), 'hearing' (akoē), 'acceptable' (dektos). The disputed status arises from distribution across the whole Bible, not from textual variants, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Romans 10:14-17 as a binding chain (faith from hearing, hearing through the word of Christ), John 3:18 as grounding condemnation on not believing the named Son, and Acts 4:12 plus John 14:6 as excluding any other name and channel. On this reading the named, heard, confessed object is the only saving access and inclusivism is therefore false.

Reads Acts 10:35 (the God-fearer of every nation is 'acceptable' (dektos)), Romans 2:14-16 (conscience may defend at the judgment), Romans 4 (Abraham justified by faith without gospel content), and Hebrews 11:6 (faith that God is and rewards seekers) as showing that Christ's work can be applied through faith whose explicit object is not yet the historical Jesus. The sole-channel texts (Acts 4:12, John 14:6) fix the means as Christ without requiring conscious knowledge of him at the lexical level, so the exclusive scope is not secured by the words.

Holds that the same canon that demands hearing also calls the never-evangelized God-fearer acceptable, so the cases of those never evangelized and those before the incarnation are left open. The condemnation texts use 'to refuse to be persuaded or to disobey' (apeitheō, refusing a presented Son) and the perfect 'has been judged' (kekritai), which describe rejection of revealed content and do not by their vocabulary settle the status of one who never heard.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the covenantal arc. The Old Testament saints and Gentile God-fearers are described with saving faith whose explicit object predates or lacks the proclaimed gospel, while the post-incarnation texts tie response to the named Son. Progressive revelation is in play because the object of saving faith is presented as growing in explicitness across the canon, and the words do not state whether the fuller explicitness is retroactively required of all.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does saving access to Christ's work require conscious, explicit faith in the historical Jesus, or can that work be applied to some who respond in faith without explicit knowledge of the gospel?
stem_audit.notes: VERDICT-CHANGED: the prior file recorded affirms=true, high confidence. This file changes it to disputed, medium confidence. Reason at the word level: the canon supplies two patterns the vocabulary does not rank. One ties the saving outcome to a named, heard, confessed object (Romans 10:14-17, John 3:18, Acts 4:12). The other predicates 'acceptable' (dektos) of the God-fearer in every nation before proclamation (Acts 10:35, where 'acceptable' (dektos) is a five-occurrence term meaning acceptable not saved), grants conscience a defending verdict (Romans 2:15, 'accusing or defending' (katēgoreō ē apologeomai)), and shows faith justifying Abraham and the Hebrews 11 saints without explicit Christ-content (Romans 4:5, Hebrews 11:6 where the object is the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) 'rewarder' (misthapodotēs), God-who-rewards). The proposition asserts an exclusive scope (no saving faith apart from explicit response to the historical Jesus) that the words leave underdetermined on the cases of those never evangelized and those who lived before the incarnation. The original question also preloads its conclusion (saving faith is not granted apart from such explicit response), so the neutralized form restates it as an open question. The verdict is derived on the original question wording.

lay_summary: The Greek words give two patterns that the canon does not rank, and that is why readers divide. The first pattern ties being saved to a named, heard, spoken object. Romans 10:14-17 builds a chain in reverse: calling on the Lord assumes believing, believing assumes hearing, hearing assumes a preacher, so 'faith comes from hearing' (pistis ex akoēs) and hearing through the word of Christ. John 3:18 says the one not believing in the name of the only-begotten Son (monogenes, one-of-a-kind) 'has already been judged' (kekritai, a completed action whose result still stands), and Acts 4:12 with John 14:6 says there is no other name and no other way to the Father. Read alone, these make conscious response to the proclaimed Jesus the only door, so inclusivism would be false. The second pattern uses different words for different people. Acts 10:35 calls the God-fearer in every nation who works righteousness 'acceptable' (dektos), and that word appears only five times in the whole canon and elsewhere means welcome or acceptable, not saved, so it does not by itself say the man is finally saved. Romans 2:14-16 says Gentiles without the law do 'by nature' (physei) what the law requires and their 'conscience' (syneidēsis) may accuse or even defend them at the judgment. Romans 4 says Abraham was justified by 'believing' (pisteuō) whose stated object was the promise and the God who justifies, not the historical Jesus. Hebrews 11:6 requires only faith that God exists and rewards those who seek him, using a one-time-only word for 'rewarder' (misthapodotēs, a hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible). So the same canon both demands hearing and names a faith without the gospel's full content. The vocabulary fixes Christ as the means of salvation but never states in plain words whether a person must consciously know him to receive that salvation, and it does not settle the case of the one who never heard or who lived before the incarnation. Because the words give two unranked patterns and leave that scope open, the proposition lands as genuinely disputed rather than plainly settled.
